b: Gold is the Metal (with the Broadest Shoulders)
Assembled from the discarded off-cuts from Horse Rotorvator and the group's unused Hellraiser score, Coil's third album proves far more than the sum of its parts

Alchemy. The protoscientific transmutation of base materials into “noble metals” such as gold is a well documented theory more closely aligned with philosophical and spiritual traditions than tangible science. In Alejandro Jodorowsky’s cult work of psychedelic cinema, The Holy Mountain, the protagonist defecates in a bell jar and inhales the rotting fumes in a bid to turn himself into gold.

For Coil’s third album, Peter ‘Sleazy’ Christopherson and Geoff Rushton (AKA John Balance), joined by Stephen Thrower, scratched around on their cutting room floor to make use of the largely instrumental tracks that had been rejected for Horse Rotorvator and their abandoned Hellraiser score. For this reason, it was initially treated as slight. As a compendium of roughly thrown together odds and sods lacking in cohesion.

But, for Coil, that wasn’t the case. They viewed these snippets, ideas, and experiments as the final word in a trilogy beginning with their debut Scatology. This can be seen and heard in the opening and closing tracks, with their references to ‘The Anal Staircase’ and ‘First Five Minutes After Death’ respectively. Contrarily, the trio also referred to it as a “stop-gap and breathing space … between two twins.”

Which is where Coil existed best – in that gap between two worlds. They excelled at smearing the boundaries between high and low art. The sacred and the profane. We get a glimpse of this on ‘Cardinal Points’ where tenor and soprano choral voices serenade one another in the midst of writhing, raspy, rodent-like rhythms. Chickens cluck through Stravinsky samples on ‘The Last Rites of Spring’, and, at various points, crowd noises of a Thai boxing match puncture warped synths whilst drunken admissions are purloined from a documentary about British boxing.

Thailand was a second home for Sleazy. It’s where he chose to live after the death of his life and creative partner, Rushton. It was the location for Coil’s seemingly exploitative music video for ‘Love’s Secret Domain’, with scantily clad Thai boys cavorting for Westerners’ pleasure. It’s also where Sleazy saw his final days out.

This clash of brows is perhaps best exemplified during the interconnected tissue of ‘Aqua Regalia’ and ‘…Of Free-Enterprise’ where an utterly soused brass band’s rumpus tumbles into Richard Verge’s rendition of ‘Greensleeves’ on the E-mu Emulator. The carnivalesque clattering of imbibed abandon makes a stark contrast to the austere strings of a composition often misattributed to the femicidal, incompetent husband Henry VIII. It undercuts the pomposity, poking fun at power.

And Coil’s music was rarely a presentation of power. They didn’t go in for the muscular synths and throbbing backline of EBM. And, even when they did flirt with these aesthetics, such as on ‘The Broken Wheel’, they parody it with false starts, deconstructing the track into its constituent parts, and layering a sardonic, exaggerated sexual dialogue over the top. Their sense of overwhelm instead arrived in lopsided loops, jarring synthesizer stabs, and a general sense of the world warping around them. It swerved the trappings of Sleazy’s earlier outfit Throbbing Gristle, replacing bludgeoning distortion and screaming feedback with discordant, discombobulating drones, lolloping drums and electronics that sounded like they were hooked up to a geriatric washing machine. They also dribbled magickal and esoteric symbolism over everything.

Not to say that they didn’t occasionally dabble in harsher sound palettes – ‘Soundtrap’, ‘First Five Minutes After Violent Death’ and the accidental distorted mangling of their Fairlight synth on ‘Metal in the Head’ certainly prove that point. Gold is the Metal… provides the link to Coil’s future, signalling directions yet to come. It also has a dark streak of fun wriggling throughout it, offering a different side of Coil to Horse Rotorvator’s darkness. It’s clumsy to say but this album proves, with the right hands at the helm, you can turn shit into gold.
